mappings.note: Both statements are about the definition and discovery of dispersion by a prism - C 8.1-LO-3.
Sorts twinkling and advanced sunrise (atmospheric refraction) from the Tyndall effect (scattering); the keyed effects are C 5.3-LO-2's two named examples.
Red danger signals are seen far off because red scatters least in smoke and fog - a scattering application, C 8.1-LO-4.
The blue of deep sea water follows from the scattering that colours the sky; C 8.1-LO-4 is the only outcome about colour produced by scattering.
Names dispersion from its definition - the head clause of C 8.1-LO-3.
Red scatters least, so danger signals carry - scattering, C 8.1-LO-4. DEFECT: duplicate stem of qid:105011.
What a myopic person can still see clearly (near objects) is the defining contrast between myopia and hypermetropia in LO-5.
Names accommodation from its description - LO-4's accommodation clause.
Nature of the retinal image (real, inverted, diminished) - how the normal eye forms its image, LO-4.
Bifocals correct presbyopia, the only defect in LO-5 that spoils both near and far vision.
Which colour scatters least (red) - the wavelength dependence of scattering, C 8.1-LO-4, not prism deviation.
Focusing at different distances by changing focal length is accommodation - LO-4 verbatim.
Focal length increases when the ciliary muscles relax and the lens thins - the accommodation mechanism, LO-4.

Keyed answer is the ciliary muscles, so the outcome is LO-4's accommodation mechanism. DEFECT: the stem is corrupt - it fuses 'least distance of distinct vision' with 'change in focal length of an eye lens is caused by the action of the ...' and as written asks a question its options cannot answer.
Cooler air behaving as optically denser is the density-gradient premise of atmospheric refraction - C 5.3-LO-2, the outcome that owns that mechanism.
Image forms on the retina - structure clause of LO-4.
Character of the image in a normal eye - LO-4, since no defect is in play.
Far point of the normal eye is infinity - a limit of normal accommodation, LO-4.
Minimum distance of clear vision, 25 cm - the near point of the normal eye, LO-4.
Convex lens cures long-sightedness - LO-5's lens-selection clause.
The eye lens is convex (converging) - a structural fact about the eye, LO-4.
Blind spot and the absence of rods and cones at the optic nerve - anatomy of the retina, LO-4's structure clause. Stored concept tag 'Scattering of Light' is wrong.
An elongated eyeball is a cause of myopia, so this is defect identification, LO-5. Stored concept tag 'Human Eye Structure' would point at LO-4 and is wrong.
Type of image formed by the eye lens on the retina - LO-4.
The iris and pupil control the light admitted - structure and function of the eye, LO-4. Stored concept tag 'Scattering of Light' is wrong.
White noon sun because the short path scatters least - the scattering outcome, LO-4.
Twinkling of stars - the first example named inside C 5.3-LO-2.
Splitting of white light by a prism is dispersion - C 8.1-LO-3.
Far point at 2 m needs a -0.5 D concave lens - selecting the corrective lens, LO-5. Stored concept tag 'Power of Accommodation' is wrong.
Fog blocks vision because its droplets scatter light - scattering, C 8.1-LO-4. Stored concept tag 'Refraction through Prism' is wrong.
Names atmospheric refraction from its definition - the head clause of C 5.3-LO-2.
Names scattering from its definition - the head clause of C 8.1-LO-4, as against dispersion in LO-3.
Distant vision intact, near vision lost - hypermetropia, named in LO-5.
Concave lens corrects myopia - LO-5's lens-selection clause.
The reddish sun at sunrise and sunset is scattering, LO-4. Stored concept tag 'Advance Sunrise & Delayed Sunset' points at refraction and is wrong - the item asks about colour, not timing.

DEFECT: misfiled. This is a concave-MIRROR item (reflectors in torches, object beyond the centre of curvature) from Light: Reflection and Refraction. C 2.3 is explicitly about lenses, and no outcome in this chapter's frame is true of it, so it is cited at the goal CG 2 rather than forced onto an eye or prism outcome.
Assertion-reason on the hypermetropic near point and its corrective lens - LO-5 covers both halves, and the reason is false because the lens is convex.
The natural phenomenon caused by dispersion is the rainbow - C 8.1-LO-3 names both.
Cataract is the clouding of the eye lens - a condition of the eye's structure, LO-4. It is not one of the three refractive defects in LO-5, so LO-5 would be false.
Least distance of distinct vision for a normal eye - LO-4.
Near vision intact, distant vision lost - myopia, LO-5.
Near and far points of a young NORMAL eye - the limits of healthy accommodation, LO-4.
Cause of splitting in a prism (colour-dependent refractive index) - the mechanism of dispersion, LO-3.
Ciliary muscles change the focal length - accommodation mechanism, LO-4.
Accommodation named from its description - LO-4. DEFECT: duplicate stem of qid:105020.
Corrective lenses for both myopia and hypermetropia - LO-5's lens-selection clause across two of its three defects.
The iris as the muscular diaphragm controlling the pupil - structure clause of LO-4.
The pupil as the opening in front of the lens - structure clause of LO-4.
Retina as the part where the image forms - LO-4's structure clause.
Function of the iris in regulating light - structure and function of the eye, LO-4, not accommodation of the lens.
Full description of the eye's parts and their functions - LO-4's structure clause in its widest form.
Why the retinal image is inverted (a convex lens forming a real image) - how the normal eye forms its image, LO-4.
Tests whether the student knows most refraction happens at the cornea, not the lens - a structural fact, LO-4.
The eye as a converging system forming a real image on the retina - structure plus accommodation, both LO-4.
Labelled diagram of the eye annotated with each part's optical function - LO-4's structure clause.
Red bends least in a prism - deviation order within dispersion, LO-3.
Violet deviated most - the other end of the same LO-3 deviation order.
Names the spectrum produced by dispersion - C 8.1-LO-3.
Blue sky by scattering - the first example named in C 8.1-LO-4.
No air molecules, no scattering, black sky - the blue-sky mechanism of LO-4 in reverse.
Assertion-reason tying the blue sky to preferential scattering of short wavelengths - exactly C 8.1-LO-4.
Concave lens for myopia - LO-5's lens-selection clause.
Myopia explained with causes and correction - all three clauses of LO-5's myopia half.
In myopia the image forms in front of the retina - the defining mechanism of the defect, LO-5, not the normal-eye behaviour of LO-4.

Matches myopia, hypermetropia and presbyopia to their lenses - LO-5's 'selects the type of lens that corrects each' in one item. Astigmatism/cylindrical is outside the outcome but is only one of four pairs.
Ciliary muscles as the agent of accommodation - LO-4.
Accommodation and the near/far point limits within which it works - LO-4's accommodation clause and its bounds.
Numerical range of accommodation power (40 D to 44 D) for a NORMAL eye - an accommodation calculation, LO-4. No defect is corrected, so LO-5 would be false.
Least distance of distinct vision for a normal adult - LO-4.
Near point of a normal adult eye is 25 cm - LO-4.
Power of the lens correcting a far point of 80 cm - selecting and sizing the corrective lens for myopia, LO-5, in contrast with the accommodation calculation at qid:707317.
Dispersion happens because colours have different refractive indices in glass - the mechanism inside LO-3.
How a prism disperses and how Newton proved the colours are in the light - C 8.1-LO-3.
Full account of rainbow formation naming each optical effect in order - the rainbow clause of C 8.1-LO-3.
Newton's two-prism experiment as a proof rather than a demonstration - dispersion through a prism, LO-3.
Stars twinkle, planets do not, because a planet is an extended source - the atmospheric-refraction outcome C 5.3-LO-2.
Assertion-reason on planets not twinkling - the same atmospheric-refraction outcome, LO-2 of C 5.3.
Sun visible two minutes early - the advanced-sunrise example named in C 5.3-LO-2.
Red for danger signals because it scatters least - a scattering application, LO-4.
The Tyndall effect is scattering by suspended particles - LO-4's head clause, 'Explains the scattering of light'.

Tyndall effect used to tell a colloid from a true solution; the physics being examined is still scattering, C 8.1-LO-4. Cited there rather than at a competency because the outcome's head clause covers explaining scattering, not only the sky examples.
Presbyopia and its cause - the third defect named in LO-5.
Assertion-reason on correcting presbyopia; requires knowing it needs bifocals, not a single concave lens - LO-5's lens-selection clause.
Near point at 50 cm names hypermetropia and its convex lens - LO-5.
Hypermetropia explained and contrasted with myopia - LO-5 covers both defects, so one code suffices.
Power of the convex lens that brings the near point back to 25 cm - sizing the corrective lens, LO-5.
Why a prism deviates and a parallel-faced slab does not - the prism geometry that makes dispersion visible, LO-3.
Full labelled prism ray diagram with every angle - the ray-diagram requirement of C 8.1-LO-3.
The three effects in a raindrop - the rainbow clause of LO-3. Scattering is not among them, so LO-4 is false.
A rainbow is seen opposite the sun - a geometric consequence of the rainbow account in LO-3.
Reddening of the sun near the horizon - the second example named in C 8.1-LO-4.
Scattering explained and applied to the blue sky, white clouds and red sunset - all three sit inside LO-4.
How particle size relative to wavelength decides the observed colour - the mechanism of scattering, LO-4, at its most general.

A four-pair match that deliberately crosses the chapter's three mechanisms: blue sky and white clouds need scattering (C 8.1-LO-4), twinkling needs atmospheric refraction (C 5.3-LO-2), the rainbow needs dispersion and internal reflection (C 8.1-LO-3). No single outcome answers it, and all three are indispensable.
Atmospheric refraction explained and used for the twinkling of stars and advanced sunrise - C 5.3-LO-2 word for word.
The item's whole point is keeping atmospheric refraction and scattering apart across four phenomena, so both outcomes are needed; dropping either leaves half the answer unreachable.
Corrects the misconception that a star's brightness really varies - the twinkling half of C 5.3-LO-2.
Defines the angle of deviation of a prism - the prism geometry underpinning C 8.1-LO-3.
